**Reply:** We thank the reviewer for asking about the methodology behind Tables 8 and 9. Both tables are based on controlled microbenchmarks that measure a single forward pass of the dense and pruned models under identical conditions.

Concretely, on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU, we switch to evaluation mode and construct a synthetic input batch of size 1 with sequence length 2048 by sampling token IDs uniformly from the model’s vocabulary. The pruning framework extends the OBS idea to the SSM portion of a Mamba model, along with some well motivated ideas on how to prune other parts of the network based on sensitivity (this reminded me of how a work like LLM.int8() handles outlier weights during quantization).

While the paper has certain promising ideas, it also contains several flaws in soundness and practicality in the current form that make me lean towards rejection.

The paper instead focuses on the SSM layers instead, which (especially in Mamba2) have much lesser impact on the overall efficiency (in both parallel scan and recurrent inference modes). At the very least, the writing should be made clearer to reflect this so that this does not mislead the eventual reader.

- The authors seem aware of the above limitation and did try to investigate pruning the in_proj, out_proj, and other layers (in section 3.4 and in B.2.3), however the results incur a significant performance drop.

- When I compare the dense Mamba-1.4B model to the pruned Mamba-2.8B model, I see similar or worse performance (for both downstream evals and runtime efficiency) for the pruned larger model. summary.value: This paper proposes SparseSSM, the first training-free, one-shot pruning framework designed specifically for Mamba-based state-space models.

strengths.value: This paper clearly presents its method and provides comprehensive numerical results across multiple Mamba checkpoints, demonstrating consistent performance retention under high sparsity levels. The proposed SparseSSM method is conceptually sound, extending the Optimal Brain Surgeon framework to selective state-space models in a theoretically grounded way. The layer-wise Hessian-based importance estimation and time-weighted aggregation strategy are well-motivated and novel in the context of SSMs. Furthermore, the empirical results convincingly show that SparseSSM can prune up to 50% of weights without fine-tuning or noticeable accuracy degradation, which is a strong practical advantage. The method’s ability to generalize across both Mamba-1 and Mamba-2 architectures also highlights its robustness and general applicability.

weaknesses.value: While the proposed SparseSSM method is well-motivated and empirically effective, several important aspects remain insufficiently addressed. First, since Mamba and other state-space models already benefit from efficient recurrent inference, it is unclear whether pruning further improves real-world inference speed or hardware efficiency. The paper does not provide detailed runtime, memory, or energy analyses to substantiate the claimed computational benefits. Second, evaluating performance solely on language modeling and zero-shot benchmarks may not fully capture the potential trade-offs introduced by sparsity—especially regarding numerical stability and robustness under low-precision or long-sequence settings. A more comprehensive discussion of how sparsity affects runtime performance, stability, and generalization beyond standard benchmarks would greatly strengthen the paper’s empirical rigor and practical relevance.

questions.value: This paper proposes SparseSSM for one-shot pruning of Mamba-based models. While the results demonstrate negligible performance degradation under various sparsity levels, the paper does not clearly quantify the corresponding computational savings. It would be valuable to report metrics such as inference latency, energy efficiency, or throughput speedups to substantiate the claimed efficiency benefits.

> *I am also not fully convinced by the reported speedups of the “recurrent mode.” The practical scenarios where this mode offers advantages seem limited. First, Mamba2 already proposes an efficient algorithm for computing the recurrent formulation of the state-space equation via matrix multiplications. Second, even on CPU, MKL leverages SIMD instructions and multi-core parallelism, which significantly accelerates matrix operations. Finally, the speedups of the Parallel Scan Mode using custom CUDA kernels also appear limited, leaving the motivation behind the proposed method unclear.*

**Reply:** We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments and the opportunity to clarify our focus and experimental design.

First, our method is primarily designed as an **unstructured pruning** framework that extends classical OBS-style algorithms to Mamba architectures. Traditional OBS methods and mainstream frameworks such as SparseGPT [1] are also unstructured pruning methods, and SparseGPT itself does not mainly target runtime acceleration but rather demonstrates that large Transformer models can be pruned in a training-free manner. In the same spirit, our paper focuses on showing that Mamba models can likewise be pruned in a training-free, unstructured way. The design of highly optimized custom kernels to fully exploit these sparsity patterns is intentionally left beyond the scope of this work.

Second, regarding the reported speedups:

- In many realistic deployment scenarios such as edge devices or **environments without NVIDIA GPUs**, the specialized CUDA kernels for Mamba-1/2 are not available. For this reason, we evaluate speedups under the native, framework-provided implementation of the architecture, which we believe better reflects these non-ideal but practically relevant settings.
- The observed speedups mainly come from our structured extension of the proposed method. We emphasize that we only explore structured pruning for the SSM modules and report the corresponding acceleration. Even in this limited setting, pruning the SSM component yields up to **1.72×** speedup for the SSM module, which we regard as a substantial gain. For the whole model, we prune only a relatively small subset of the overall model parameters yet already obtain measurable end-to-end speedups.
- We further evaluate the acceleration of Mamba models on **CPU**, where specialized GPU kernels are not applicable and the benefits of reducing the recurrent computation become more evident, see Tab. 2.

summary.value: This paper presents \modelname, a training-free, one-shot pruning technique for Mamba-based state-space language models. The method adapts the Optimal Brain Surgeon framework to accommodate the time-shared and discretized nature of the state-transition matrix in selective state-space modules, and incorporates a sensitivity-based approach for pruning feed-forward network components. The authors report that their algorithm can prune up to 50% of SSM weights without fine-tuning and with no observed drop in zero-shot accuracy, outperforming several baseline pruning strategies. The work offers a modest contribution to efficient compression of state-space models as an extension to an existing method.

strengths.value:
Originality: The paper introduces an extension to the OBS pruning framework tailored to Mamba-based state-space models, addressing architectural challenges—like time-shared and discretized parameters—not considered in prior work. 

Quality: The approach has rigorous theoretical derivations and an empirical evaluation spanning different model sizes, pruning granularities, and both language modeling and reasoning benchmarks. The inclusion of ablation studies and sensitivity analyses validates the method’s effectiveness and robustness.

Clarity: The presentation is clear and organized, offering step-by-step explanations and visual aids that facilitate understanding of both the technical challenges and solutions. Key concepts and distinctions from prior work are well-articulated.

Significance: Efficient pruning of SSMs is practically important as these models see wider use. Achieving high sparsity without accuracy loss makes deployment more feasible and compression methods are important in this emerging area.

weaknesses.value:
1. Limited Baseline Comparison: The experimental evaluation primarily contrasts the proposed method with magnitude pruning, SparseGPT, and Mamba-Shedder. However, recent pruning approaches such as Wanda are not included. Further evaluation would clarify whether the paper’s architectural adaptations are essential and show real empirical advantages.

2. Experimental Scope and Generalization: Although multiple scales of Mamba models are evaluated, the experiments are limited to Mamba architecture alone. The claim that OBS-style pruning generalizes to state-space models would be much stronger if demonstrated on alternative SSMs (e.g., S4 or S5) and hybrid models (e.g., JAMBA, Zamba). Additionally, assessing the robustness of the pruning method under longer context lengths or distributional shifts—key strengths of SSMs—would provide more convincing evidence of practical utility.

3. Evaluation Metrics and Practical Impact: The focus is primarily on perplexity and zero-shot accuracy. The benefits of pruning for deployment (such as latency, memory savings, or throughput improvements) are asserted but not quantified. Structured pruning is said to improve efficiency, but actual hardware speedup, resource consumption, or inference time should be reported across diverse sparsity settings, ideally with comparisons to pruned transformer models.

4. Theoretical Clarification: The adaptation of Hessian-based saliency scores to time-shared and discretized SSM parameters is reasonable, but the discussion could more thoroughly explain why generic second-order pruning (such as SparseGPT) fails or underperforms in this context, both mathematically and experimentally. Demonstrating fundamental limitations or failure cases of alternative methods would strengthen the motivation for the approach.

We sincerely thank the reviewer `oBAu` for the careful and detailed assessment. Below we restate each concern and question and respond in turn.

> **(W1 & Q1):** *In SSM-based models, most parameters typically reside in the input and output projection layers, which also tend to be the primary latency bottlenecks during generation. The paper focuses on pruning the state transition matrix A, but the motivation and practical impact of pruning this component are not entirely clear.* 

*Would the authors provide more insight into why pruning the state transition matrix A is particularly important or beneficial compared to pruning the input and output projection layers, which typically dominate both the parameter count and runtime cost in SSM-based architectures?*

**Reply:** We thank the reviewer for highlighting the question. While it is true that most parameters reside in these projection layers, the state-space mixer is invoked at every time step, so its recurrent updates account for a substantial fraction of the runtime in generation, even though its parameter count is smaller. SSM block is not negligible in the overall latency, especially in recurrent mode. Pruning the SSM module directly reduces both the cost of these updates and the size of the recurrent state. As shown in the **Tab. 1** below, the selective scan accounts for a large portion of the inference time.

As shown in **Tables 8 and 9 in our Appendix B.2.4–B.2.5**, pruning 50% of the A parameters leads to substantial gains in recurrent mode: we observe roughly 1.6~2.2x end-to-end speedup together with close to 50% reduction in peak memory usage, despite touching only a small fraction of the total parameters.

Moreover, our framework is **not limited to SSM layer**, we perform component-wise sensitivity analysis and extend pruning to other linear layers and in this full-model setting SparseSSM still yields better accuracy-sparsity trade-offs than existing training-free baselines.

**Tab. 1**: Contribution of Each Module to Inference Latency in Mamba-370m

| **Module** | **Parallel scan mode (ms)** | **Recurrent mode (ms)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| selective scan | 5.530 | 535.1 |
| FFN | 12.03 | 12.03 |

---

> **(W2):** *The proposed hierarchical aggregation protocol and sensitivity-aware pruning appear to be primarily heuristic, and their theoretical justification is limited. It would strengthen the work to provide more formal grounding or analytical discussion on why these mechanisms improve pruning stability or accuracy preservation.*

**Reply:** We appreciate the reviewer’s request for a clearer rationale behind both the hierarchical aggregation protocol and the sensitivity-aware pruning. 

**For the hierarchical aggregation**, we logged the hidden state at every time step and computed the expectations $H_t​=\mathbb{E}∥h_t​∥_2^2​$ across a held-out set of inputs. As illustrated in the new plots that we will add to the appendix, $H_t$ exhibits a highly consistent pattern across layers. It increases with time in a concave fashion, with fast growth at early steps and a slowly saturating tail. Consequently, most of the state information is rapidly accumulated in the early timesteps, and our power-law aggregation is designed to reflect this behavior by assigning gradually decreasing weight along the sequence. 

We have explicitly **compared** power-law aggregation with uniform and exponential alternatives in our pruning experiments and found that the power-law choice consistently yields the best perplexity and zero-shot accuracy at matched sparsity levels.

**Tab. 2:** Ablation study of aggregation methods

|  | Wiki. $\downarrow$ | Ptb $\downarrow$ | C4 $\downarrow$ | Avg. zero-shot accuracy $\uparrow$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| linear aggregation | 15.28 | 24.93 | 20.47 | 46.54 |
| exponential aggregation | 15.16 | 24.78 | 20.35 | 47.39 |
| **power-low aggregation (Ours)** | **15.04** | **24.63** | **20.13** | **47.47** |

**For sensitivity-aware pruning**, we observe in our experiments that different components of SSM-based models exhibit markedly different pruning tolerance (see Fig. 2 and Appendix B.2.3 in the paper), pruning the same fraction of weights in the SSM core, in-/out-projections leads to very different loss increases. 

Therefore, allocating less sparsity to high-saliency blocks and more sparsity to low-saliency ones is precisely the solution of the corresponding constrained minimization problem. Our sensitivity-aware scheme is a practical realization of this principle.

Concretely, we resize the SSM-related projections and obtain a 1.72× speedup for the SSM module itself at 50% sparsity with negligible accuracy loss (**Table 4 in the paper**), and we then propagate this design to full models and benchmark end-to-end inference.

Beyond compute savings, structured sparsity in SSM module directly translates into lower memory headroom for recurrent inference, which enables larger batch sizes or longer contexts under fixed VRAM budgets.

Demonstrating fundamental limitations or failure cases of alternative methods would strengthen the motivation for the approach.*

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. 

**Mathematically**, generic second-order pruning such as SparseGPT is derived for standard feed-forward or attention layers, where a weight matrix $W$ is applied once per layer as a linear map and the local second-order objective reduces to reconstructing layer outputs on a mini-batch. In contrast, the SSM diagonal $A_{\log}$ in Mamba is (i) time-shared across all timesteps, (ii) passed through a non-linear discretization map $A = -\exp(A_{\log})$ and further become $\Delta A$. The true second-order saliency need consideration about the discretization operation and an aggregation of Hessian contributions over all timesteps. Small perturbations of $A_{\log}$ can also produce exponentially amplified changes in the discrete eigenvalues and in long-range behavior.

**Experimentally**, this theoretical mismatch is reflected in our results on Mamba pruning. At the same sparsity levels, SparseGPT and Wanda cause severe degradation when applied to the SSM block, especially on perplexity-based language modeling benchmarks, whereas our SparseSSM keep perplexity close to the dense model and yield higher zero-shot accuracy.

Dear Area Chairs,

Thank you very much for your service to ICLR26! We respectfully submit this brief summary to assist you in evaluating our paper.

---

**Paper Summary**

While existing one-shot pruning methods are effective for generic linear and attention blocks, they fail to account for the time-shared and discretized state-transition matrix at the heart of the selective state-space module and are not designed with the overall Mamba in mind.

We propose SparseSSM, a one-shot training-free pruning framework that extends Optimal Brain Surgeon to the state-space architecture like Mamba. Our framework

- Can prune 50% of SSM weights in Mamba without fine-tuning and observe no zero-shot accuracy loss.
- Can be adapted to semi-structured and structured sparsity format and observe end-to-end speedup, and be generalized to other SSM-based architectures.
- Are supported by mathematical proofs and visualization analysis.

---

**Reviews Summary**

Before rebuttal, we received scores **6 / 2 / 6 / 6 / 4** with confidences **3 / 4 / 3 / 4 / 5**. Two reviewers (`ef7V` (6/3) and `oBAu` (4/5)) engaged in post-rebuttal discussion. `ef7V` explicitly stated that he/she was satisfied with our responses.

**Strengths**

Reviewers generally agree that:

- **Timely and important problem:** `H9zR` highlights that “efficient pruning of SSMs is practically important”, `bdWM` notes that achieving high sparsity “is a strong practical advantage.”
- **Technical Novelty:** `ef7V` calls our method a “novel technical adaptation” and `H9zR` stresses the “originality” of extending second-order pruning to Mamba SSMs, while `bdWM` describes SparseSSM as “conceptually sound”.
- **Comprehensive and convincing experiments:** Reviewers `bdWM` , `ef7V` , `oBAu`, `Qd5q` highlight our comprehensive experiments. `ef7V` highlights “comprehensive experiments – multiple model sizes, datasets, and sparsity regimes”.
- **Practical value in the training-free regime:** Reviewers `ef7V`,  `H9zR`, `Qd5q` agree that a one-shot method with negligible training cost is useful for deployment. `Qd5q` highlights that the method is “training-free, making it tractable to apply to pretrained models in an inexpensive way.”

---

**Weaknesses and Responses**

Below we briefly summarize the main concerns and our rebuttal actions.

> *Application scope appears limited (Reviewers `Qd5q`, `oBAu`, `H9zR`)*

- We added results for larger checkpoints including Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B, and 8B, see Appendix B.2.6.
- We applied our training-free framework to vision via **MambaVision** and validated hybrid architecture applicability by pruning **Jamba**, see Appendix B.2.7.

> *Missing benchmarks and baselines (Reviewers `Qd5q`, `H9zR`, `ef7V`)*

- We added Wanda as a modern training-free baseline, see Table 1.
- We expanded our evaluation to the FineWeb dataset and Long-context language modeling, see Appendix B.2.6.

> *Acceleration seems modest and configuration details were unclear* (**concern of `oBAu` (rating 4)**)

We clarified our primary goal: SparseSSM is designed as a training-free unstructured OBS-style pruning framework. In line with SparseGPT and similar work, our main emphasis is on preserving accuracy at high sparsity in a one-shot setting, rather than designing for maximal raw speedup.

Moreover, our **structured extension** does yield native measurable acceleration, see Table 3 and Apendix B.2.4.

- We clarified the experimental setup.
- In recurrent mode or on CPU, pruning gives substantial end-to-end speedups.
- In parallel scan, pruning a relatively small fraction of parameters leads to measurable latency reductions.

> *Focusing on SSM despite its smaller parameter share* (**concern of  `Qd5q` (rating 2)**)

The SSM block is architecturally unique in Mamba and is time-shared. Despite its smaller parameter count, it contributes a non-trivial portion of runtime. We accordingly revised the motivation in the Introduction.

Our framework is **not restricted to SSM,** we perform sensitivity analysis and prune all modules. SparseSSM still yields the best performance when aggressively pruning the whole architecture, see Section 3.4 and Appendix B.2.1.

> *Insufficient justification for temporal aggregation and sensitivity-aware pruning (Reviewers `ef7V`, `oBAu`)*

We added visual analyses for each to support our methods, see Figures 2 and 3. We also added an ablation study comparing, see Appendix B.2.8.

> *Concerns about pruning stability (Reviewers `ef7V`, `bdWM`)*

We conducted both static and dynamic eigenvalue analysis to address stability.

> *Other detailed concerns*

We provided point-by-point clarifications for the reviewers’ remaining concerns.

---

We believe that the extensive new experiments and clarifications in our rebuttal have effectively addressed the concerns.

We sincerely thank all the reviewers for their valuable feedback and for improving our paper. We are also deeply grateful to the Area Chairs for your precious time!

Best,

Authors

summary.value: This paper proposes SparseSSM, a training-free OBS-style pruning framework for Mamba-based SSM models. The key technical contribution is Theorem 1, which derives the Hessian for the time-shared, discretized state-transition matrix A,a non-trivial extension since the same matrix is reused across time steps. Strengths include the novel Hessian derivation, comprehensive experiments across model sizes, and strong results at 50% SSM sparsity with minimal accuracy loss. However, there is a fundamental practical limitation: most of Mamba parameters reside in the in_proj/out_proj projection layers, not the SSM. In common deployment regimes (parallel scan on GPU), pruning SSM yields only ~1.05x speedup. The recurrent mode shows better speedups (1.7-2x) but is a less common use case. When pruning the larger projection layers (where SparseGPT would apply), performance degrades significantly. Thus, the setting where SSM pruning provides meaningful end-to-end gains has not been convincingly demonstrated.

We sincerely thank the reviewer `ef7V` for the very encouraging and detailed assessment, for highlighting both the strengths and the limitations of our current submission. Below we restate each weakness and question and provide a point-by-point response.

---

> **(W1 & Q1):** *Temporal aggregation lacks theoretical grounding – The power-law choice is ad hoc; no comparison with exponential or learned weighting. What theoretical or empirical reasoning supports the power-law aggregation form? Have exponential or learned schemes been tested?*

**Reply:** We thank the reviewer for raising this point about the temporal aggregation scheme. To better justify this design, we **conducted an additional analysis** of the SSM dynamics in the trained Mamba-1 model. For each layer, we logged the hidden state at every time step and computed the expectations $H_t​=\mathbb{E}∥h_t​∥_2^2​$ across a held-out set of inputs. 

As illustrated in the new plots that we will add to the appendix, $H_t$ exhibits a highly consistent pattern across layers. It increases with time in a concave fashion, with fast growth at early steps and a slowly saturating tail. Consequently, most of the state information is rapidly accumulated in the early timesteps, and our power-law aggregation is designed to reflect this behavior by assigning gradually decreasing weight along the sequence.

In contrast, an **exponential weighting** ($\gamma^{t}$, where t is the timestep index) is sensitive to the parameter using, and a **learned weighting** would conflict with our training-free pruning setting.

**Finally**, we have explicitly **compared** power-law aggregation with uniform and exponential alternatives in our pruning experiments and found that the power-law choice consistently yields the best perplexity and zero-shot accuracy at matched sparsity levels.

**Tab. 1:** Ablation study of aggregation methods

|  | Wiki. $\downarrow$ | Ptb $\downarrow$ | C4 $\downarrow$ | Avg. zero-shot accuracy $\uparrow$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| linear aggregation | 15.28 | 24.93 | 20.47 | 46.54 |
| exponential aggregation | 15.16 | 24.78 | 20.35 | 47.39 |
| **power-low aggregation (Ours)** | **15.04** | **24.63** | **20.13** | **47.47** |

---

> **(W2 & Q4):** *Scalability and robustness – Performance drops at larger model scales; no analysis of failure modes or eigenvalue stability. Have you examined eigenvalue distributions pre-/post-pruning to confirm stability of the selective SSM dynamics?*

**Reply:** We appreciate the reviewer’s concern about scalability and robustness. To address this, we performed both static and dynamic eigenvalue analyses of the SSM blocks pre-/post- pruning.

For the **static analysis**, we inspect the diagonal $A_{\log}$ in each layer and form the continuous-time matrix $A = -\exp(A_{\log})$ (negative diagonal, hence stable), together with a conservative discrete-time approximation $\lambda_{\mathrm{disc}} = \exp(A)$ corresponding to $\Delta t = 1$. We found that pruning reduces the magnitude of the continuous-time eigenvalues and slightly shifts the discrete eigenvalue distribution toward slower but still strictly stable modes, rather than pushing the system into an unstable regime.

We also run a **dynamic analysis** in which we record the per-step discrete eigenvalues $\Delta A_t$ produced by the actual discretization during forward passes on held-out data. The empirical distributions of $\lvert \Delta A \rvert$ for dense and pruned models likewise remain below 1 across layers and timesteps, confirming that the pruned SSM does not suffer from eigenvalue instability in practice.

Taken together, these results indicate that our method will keep the stability after pruning. We will add the static and dynamic eigenvalue plots to the appendix, summarize the above statistics, and include a short discussion.
